questions.q: What does a Snowflake TASK do?
options: Runs a single SQL statement or stored procedure call on a schedule you define, with no external scheduler required
Permanently stores a copy of a table's data
Replaces the need for a virtual warehouse
Automatically writes SQL queries for you
questions.explain: A TASK is Snowflake's native scheduler — it runs SQL or a procedure on a schedule, without needing cron or an external orchestrator like Airflow.

questions.q: What state is a newly created task in, and what must you do before it actually runs?
options: It's created SUSPENDED; you must run ALTER TASK ... RESUME to turn it on
It starts running immediately upon creation with no further action
It runs once immediately, then deletes itself
It requires a separate warehouse to be manually started every time
questions.explain: Tasks are created suspended by default — a common gotcha — and need an explicit ALTER TASK ... RESUME before they'll run on schedule.

questions.q: Where would you check whether a task's scheduled runs have been succeeding or failing?
options: The task's Run History tab in Snowsight, which lists scheduled time, status, and duration for each run
There is no way to see a task's run history in Snowflake
Only by contacting Snowflake support
In the warehouse's billing statement only
questions.explain: Snowsight's task Run History tab shows every scheduled execution with its status (e.g. Succeeded or Failed) and duration.

questions.q: What does `WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('orders_stream')` accomplish on a task?
options: It lets the task skip its run entirely — and avoid spinning up its warehouse — when the paired stream has no new data
It permanently deletes the stream after each run
It forces the task to always run regardless of the stream's contents
It converts the stream into a table
questions.explain: SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA is a cheap check used in a task's WHEN clause so the task (and its warehouse) only does work when there's actually something new to process.

questions.q: Besides a fixed interval like `'60 MINUTE'`, what other schedule syntax does a Snowflake TASK support?
options: Standard cron syntax, e.g. `'USING CRON 0 * * * * UTC'`
Only fixed intervals are supported — no other syntax exists
Natural language schedules like 'every weekday morning'
Tasks cannot be scheduled at all — only triggered manually
questions.explain: TASK schedules accept either a fixed interval or cron syntax for more specific timing needs.
